Scores that share a sample

Catalog stamp 20260923. In the four AUC models below, cohort means the sample set.

Several scores can sit on one sample set. Different sample-set ids can still be the same study, including UK Biobank and Genes & Health. The average of all scores treats those evaluations as independent, so its interval is too narrow.

The four AUC models change the residual only. They do not put in the covariance between the European evaluations, or between the non-European evaluations, of scores that share a sample.

The covariance is built with vcalc, once for the European source and once for the non-European source. rma.mv fits the ancestry difference. robust gives a cluster-robust interval when the degrees of freedom are at least 4. This follows Pustejovsky & Tipton (2022) and the metafor manual page for dependent estimates. The paper is the one to confirm with Pirmin.

With one sharing group, the interval depends on the assumed ρ. The reported intervals use ρ = 0.6. Figure 9 draws ρ = 0, 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9. Five comparisons change whether the interval excludes zero from 0 to 0.9. Two of those still change between 0.3 and 0.9. 23 of the 24 comparisons with shared samples are one sharing group. 10 of 24 still exclude zero under the covariance model. The model is only for comparisons whose scores share people. The others keep the average of all scores. Shared samples alone widen the intervals 1.0–2.6×; the rest comes from variance between scores.

The linked-group bound, which puts ρ on every pair that shares any study, does not change whether any interval excludes zero. 12 of the 24 comparisons have only 2–3 scores and are flagged unstable for the between-score variance.

Worked comparisons

The figures walk through one comparison, type 2 diabetes, South Asian participants, European-only training, and bring in the other comparisons where that example cannot show the step.

Each box is one step. The robust box is the one comparison with four sharing groups: 2.3 degrees of freedom, below the threshold of 4.

The ancestry difference, both labels, and the variance on each side. The non-European side dominates the variance.

The model treats two sample-set ids with the same study name as the same people. PSS011749 and PSS004315 are different sample sets that share the label UK Biobank.

The correlation pattern is separate from the standard errors. V is the sum of the European and non-European covariances.

The curve holds when every score shares one label on both sides, or the shared side carries the variance. Points above the curve contain scores without a shared exact label.

The worked comparison has a peak. Breast cancer, Hispanic or Latin American participants, European-only training is marked σ² = 0.

Plain average, correlation only, the full model, and the linked fit. These shares are why the estimate moves.

Shared samples widen the interval, and the between-score variance widens it further.

Five comparisons change their zero call from ρ = 0 to 0.9. Two of those still change between 0.3 and 0.9. For type 2 diabetes, East Asian participants, European-only training, the estimate changes sign and excludes zero on the other side at ρ = 0.9. That is extreme weights, not stronger evidence.

ρ is the correlation of two scores' AUC errors on one side with the same label. The line is the rule for the ancestry differences. This is a sampling model.

The average of all scores, the smallest standard error, one score per sample set, and the covariance model. The sample-set term is not drawn.

Context: four AUC models on type 2 diabetes

These four models are the ones Nikolaus wrote down. They stay here as context. They are not the answer to the dependence question.

The input I need: which of the four models should account for several PGS evaluated on the same sample set, or whether you would rather drop rows than model the sharing.
  • lm(AUC ~ ancestry + PGS)
  • lm(AUC ~ ancestry + PGS, weights = 1/SE^2)
  • lmer(AUC ~ ancestry + PGS + (1|cohort), weights = 1/SE^2)
  • lmer(AUC ~ ancestry + (1|PGS) + (1|cohort), weights = 1/SE^2)

An evaluation is one AUC: one PGS, one sample set, one ancestry group, and one standard error. The sample-set term marks which evaluations share a sample set. It does not make the AUCs independent.

The four models are fit on type 2 diabetes. They can separate an ancestry group from a sample set only when a comparison uses more than one target sample set. Nine comparisons do. Seven are type 2 diabetes. The other two are breast cancer, European-only training: South Asian participants, and East Asian participants.

Eighteen comparisons have several PGS and one target sample set. Ancestry group and sample set are the same column there. The four models are not for that case. Five comparisons have one PGS.

South Asian comparison

Europeans and South Asian participants, European-only training. Thirteen PGS, eleven of them on one UK Biobank sample set.

  • Average of all scores (All PGS IVW): 0.0007 (-0.0032 to 0.0046).
  • Check, one score per target sample set: -0.0160 (-0.0223 to -0.0098).

Two comparisons

South Asian participants, European-only training, are one of the nine. Thirteen scores, eleven of them on PSS011749. The average of all scores and one score per sample set are in the box above.

Hispanic or Latin American participants, European-only training, are one of the eighteen. Eleven scores, all on PSS011736, so ancestry group and sample set are the same column. The four models are not for that comparison.

Evaluation table used here

80 evaluations. 19 PGS. 29 sample sets. 12 study names. Corrected logit values from auc_ci_to_logit(). AUC models use the delta-method SE (SE_logit × AUC × (1 − AUC)). Fits are separate for each training set. European is the reference ancestry group.

South Asian sample sets in the European-only training set:

  • PSS011749 — UK Biobank (UKB), 11 evaluation(s)
  • PSS004315 — UK Biobank (UKB), 1 evaluation(s)
  • PSS011249 — Genes & Health (G&H), 1 evaluation(s)
  • PSS011291 — UK Biobank (UKB), 1 evaluation(s)

Sample-set term, PGS fixed: lmer(AUC ~ ancestry + PGS + (1|cohort), weights = 1/SE^2)

In this model, cohort is the sample set. Evaluations from the same sample set share an offset, and the PGS stays a fixed intercept. Eleven South Asian PGS share PSS011749, and all of them are South Asian, so the sample-set offset and the ancestry coefficient compete for the same shift.

If dropping rows is preferred to modelling the sharing

Two ways to drop rows, counted on the 71 type 2 diabetes evaluations. The page does not pick one.

  • One PGS per sample set, the lowest PGS identifier: keeps 34 evaluations, drops 46 of 80.
  • The largest sample set when one PGS is evaluated more than once in an ancestry group: keeps 74 evaluations, drops 6 of 80.
If you would rather drop rows than model the sharing, which rule do you prefer: one PGS per sample set, or the largest sample set when one PGS is evaluated more than once?
